warmup.q: A join runs as 16 tasks at the same time, like 16 tills. One shop has 30% of all the payments, so the task that gets that shop has about 8 times as many rows as the middle task. The other 15 tasks take about 40 ms each. About how long does the whole join take?
options: About 40 ms, because the tasks run at the same time
About 16 x 40 = 640 ms, because the tasks run one after another
About 8 x 40 ms: as long as the one task that got the big shop
About 40 ms, because Spark spreads the big shop's rows over all 16 tasks
warmup.why: Spark sends every row of one key to one task, so the task that owns the big shop fetches about 346,000 rows while the middle task fetches about 43,000: 8 times as many. A join ends when its last task ends, so everyone waits for the slow till. Spark doesn't spread one key over many tasks by itself. AQE's skew handling and salting, in the third section, do that, and the demo there measures all of it.

sections.h: How Spark's optimizer rewrites a query, one rule at a time
sections.html:
Let's start with a question from the team that hunts for fraud: card payments from the Netherlands over 1,000 euros, at shops with category code 5001. A category code is a number that says what kind of shop it is. The demo's codes run from 5000 to 5019, and they're made up. Here it is in SQL, the language most databases use for questions about tables:

SELECT m.merchant_name, p.amount_cents
FROM payments p JOIN merchants m ON p.merchant_id = m.merchant_id
WHERE p.card_country = 'NL' AND m.mcc = 5001 AND p.amount_cents > 100 * 1000

FROM ... JOIN ... ON matches each payment (p) with its shop (m; the code calls shops merchants). WHERE keeps the rows that pass all three tests, and SELECT names the two columns to send back.

Read literally, the query says: join every payment to its shop, then keep the rows that match. Version 1 runs it that way. The join handles all 1,000,000 payments with all six of their columns, and the filter then throws away about 996 rows in every 1,000. One card in 8 is Dutch, one shop in 20 has code 5001, and 60% of amounts are above 100,000 cents. A person would filter each table first and carry only the three columns the answer needs. Version 2 is a program that makes those edits for every query, by itself.

That program is Catalyst, Spark's optimizer, the part that decides how a query should run. It holds a query as a tree of steps, called operators. Each step sits above the steps that feed it: here a Filter with a Join under it, and a table at each bottom end. A rule is a small function that takes a tree, looks for one pattern and returns a rewritten tree. PushDownPredicates looks for a filter above a join, splits its condition at each AND, and moves each part down to the table whose columns it tests. ColumnPruning removes columns that no step above uses. ConstantFolding works out 100 * 1000 once, instead of once per row. Catalyst runs groups of rules again and again, until a pass changes nothing.

explain("extended") prints the four forms the query goes through:

  1. Parsed: the tree as you wrote it. Names carry a quote mark, as in 'UnresolvedRelation [payments], because nothing has been looked up yet.
  2. Analyzed: names looked up in the catalog, Spark's list of tables and their columns. payments becomes a table of Parquet files (a file format that stores each column on its own) with six typed columns. A misspelled column fails here, before any work runs.
  3. Optimized: rules applied. The filter is split three ways: card_country = 'NL' and amount_cents > 100000 go down the payments side, and mcc = 5001 goes down the shops side. Another rule, InferFiltersFromConstraints, adds isnotnull(merchant_id): a payment with no shop number can never match a shop, so it can go early.
  4. Physical: each step becomes an operator that can run. The shops are few, so the join becomes a broadcast hash join, which copies the small table to every task (The shuffle, partitioning and joins). The scan gets PushedFilters and a three-column ReadSchema: the file reader is told to skip what fails the filter and to read three columns only. That's the pushdown from lesson 5, Columnar files: Parquet internals and pushdown.

When the plan runs, Spark fuses steps that can work on the same rows one after another. The *(1) in front of them means it wrote one Java method for the whole chain, so a row doesn't travel through a separate call for every step.

In the Try it, Spark tried 100 optimizer rules on this query, and 6 changed it. Catalyst has two blind spots. It can't see inside your own code. A Kotlin lambda (a function written inline) or a UDF (a function you register for queries to call) is closed to it, so no filter is pushed through it. The next lesson, Spark 4 for JVM engineers, shows this. And every choice in step 4 rests on size estimates. Next, we'll see what happens when they're wrong.

try.title: Watch the filter move
steps: From the labs folder, run OptimizerDemo. It sets up a million payments and 500 shops as tables, plans the fraud team's query and prints the four plans, without running anything.
Before you read: in the optimized plan, which side of the join will mcc = 5001 be on, and what will 100 * 1000 have become?
Compare the Filter in the analyzed plan with the ones in the optimized plan. Which rule in the list at the end made each change?

code.title: OptimizerDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.batch.l08.demo import scala.jdk.javaapi.CollectionConverters /** * One SQL query through Catalyst's four plans, and the optimizer rules that changed it. Nothing * runs: explain() only plans. */ fun main() { val spark = demoSpark() demoPayments(spark).createOrReplaceTempView("payments") demoMerchants(spark).createOrReplaceTempView("merchants") val df = spark.sql( """ SELECT m.merchant_name, p.amount_cents FROM payments p JOIN merchants m ON p.merchant_id = m.merchant_id WHERE p.card_country = 'NL' AND m.mcc = 5001 AND p.amount_cents > 100 * 1000 """.trimIndent() ) val qe = df.queryExecution() println("== 1. parsed: your words, nothing looked up yet ==") println(clean(qe.logical())) println("== 2. analyzed: names resolved against the catalog ==") println(clean(qe.analyzed())) println("== 3. optimized: rewritten by rules ==") println(clean(qe.optimizedPlan())) println("== 4. physical: the operators that will run ==") println(clean(qe.executedPlan())) val prefix = "org.apache.spark.sql.catalyst.optimizer." val fired = CollectionConverters.asJava(qe.tracker().rules()) .filter { (name, s) -> name.startsWith(prefix) && s.numEffectiveInvocations() > 0 } .keys.map { it.removePrefix(prefix) }.sorted() val tried = CollectionConverters.asJava(qe.tracker().rules()).keys.count { it.startsWith(prefix) } println("optimizer rules tried: $tried, rules that changed the plan: ${fired.size}") fired.forEach { println(" $it") } spark.stop() }

The parsed plan has the whole Filter above the Join, with quoted names that nothing has looked up yet. In the optimized plan the filter is gone from the top. The payments side has card_country = NL and amount_cents > 100000 (the 100 * 1000 was worked out), plus isnotnull checks that InferFiltersFromConstraints added. The shops side has the mcc test, pushed all the way down to the Range that makes up the demo's shops. A Project [merchant_id, amount_cents], a step that keeps only those columns, now sits on the payments side: ColumnPruning dropped the other four. The physical scan reads three columns, those two plus card_country, which the filter needs. Optimizer$FinishAnalysis cleaned up what analysis left behind, such as the SubqueryAlias and View wrappers.

sections.h: Changing the plan halfway: AQE uses real sizes at each shuffle
sections.html:
Catalyst plans before a single row is read, so it plans from estimates. For a file, the estimate is its size on disk. After a filter, Spark usually can't tell how many rows survive, so it keeps the estimate of the whole input.

The Try it shows how far off that can be. It looks for payments made with cards that also made one very large payment. So it joins a million payments with the payments over 2,499 euros, on card_id, the card's number. The planner estimates the flagged side at 3.9 MiB (about 4 MB): the two columns it reads, as if the filter kept every row. It really has 747 rows. Spark broadcasts a side whose estimate is below spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold. The demo's tables are about a thousand times smaller than a real day of payments, so it lowers that limit from 10 MB to 1 MB to match. Now 3.9 MiB looks too big, and Spark plans a sort-merge join, which shuffles both tables by key and sorts them (The shuffle, partitioning and joins).

A supermarket manager decides how many tills to open from last week's numbers. A careful one also walks the floor at ten o'clock and moves staff to where the queues really are. Version 1 is the first manager: plan once and live with it. That's Spark with AQE off: both sides shuffled and sorted, for a table of 747 rows.

Version 2 is the careful manager: plan again once you know. The shuffle gives Spark a natural pause. A shuffle is the step that moves rows between tasks so that rows with the same key meet. Every map task, the kind that writes the shuffle's files, must finish before any reduce task, the kind that reads them, can start. So when the last map task is done, the driver (the program that plans the job) knows exactly how many bytes went to each reduce task. Adaptive query execution (AQE), on by default since Spark 3.2, uses that pause. It cuts the physical plan into query stages at every Exchange, Spark's word for a shuffle. It runs the stages whose inputs are ready, each as a job of its own (a job is a batch of work Spark schedules in one go). Each time one finishes, AQE optimizes the rest of the plan again, with measured sizes in place of guesses. The stepper below walks through it.

At each pause, AQE can change three things. It merges small neighbouring partitions (AQEShuffleRead coalesced, from the last lesson). It switches a sort-merge join to a broadcast hash join when one side turned out smaller than spark.sql.adaptive.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold, which equals the planning limit unless you set it. And it splits skewed partitions, which is the next section. Spark 4.3 added a fourth, on by default. It turns a sort-merge join into a shuffled hash join, which skips the sort, when each partition's lookup table looks small enough to build. The labs' Spark 4.1 does that only if you set spark.sql.adaptive.maxShuffledHashJoinLocalMapThreshold.

How much does it buy? When AQE arrived in Spark 3.0, still off by default, Databricks (the company founded by Spark's creators) measured it on TPC-DS, a standard set of analytics queries. 32 queries ran more than 1.1 times faster, the best of them 8 times faster. Nearly all of that came from merging partitions and switching joins, because TPC-DS data has no skew. The skew handling paid off on real company data instead.

The plan shows all of this. Before the action (the call, such as collect(), that makes Spark run), explain() prints AdaptiveSparkPlan isFinalPlan=false and the plan from estimates. After it, you see the final plan, with ShuffleQueryStage and BroadcastQueryStage lines for the stages that ran. In the Try it, the final plan has a BroadcastHashJoin, and the run took about half as long.

The switch comes late, so it isn't free. Both map stages ran before AQE could compare the two sides. So the million payments were still written to shuffle files: 8.66 MB with AQE on, the same as with it off. AQE then reads those files where they are, with a local reader (AQEShuffleRead local), so nothing crosses the network and nothing is sorted. Here the manager picture breaks: a manager can move staff at any minute, but AQE changes the plan only between stages. Spark's tuning guide says it plainly: this is better than going on with the sort-merge join, and worse than planning the broadcast from the start. When you know a side is small, the last lesson's broadcast() hint still wins.

AQE fixes a wrong guess about a whole table. Next comes a problem it finds much harder: one key too big for its task.

try.title: See AQE switch the join
steps: From the labs folder, run AqeDemo. It prints the planner's size estimate for the flagged side and the rows it really has, then runs the same join with AQE off and on.
Predict: with AQE on, will the shuffle write go down? Will Spark run more jobs, or fewer?

code.title: AqeDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.batch.l08.demo import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.col /** * Joins a million payments with the few flagged ones on card_id. Spark's estimate for the * filtered side is megabytes; the real size is a few kilobytes. With AQE off, Spark keeps the * sort-merge join it planned. With AQE on, it re-plans after the first stages and broadcasts. */ fun main() { val spark = demoSpark() // this laptop table is 14 MB, not 14 GB: shrink the broadcast threshold from 10 MB to 1 MB to match spark.conf().set("spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold", "1MB") val log = TaskLog(spark) val payments = demoPayments(spark) val flagged = payments.where(col("amount_cents").gt(249_900)).select(col("card_id"), col("payment_id").alias("flagged_payment")) println("planner's size estimate for the flagged side: ${flagged.queryExecution().optimizedPlan().stats().simpleString()}") println("rows it really has: ${flagged.count()}") for (aqe in listOf(false, true)) { spark.conf().set("spark.sql.adaptive.enabled", aqe.toString()) fun query() = payments.join(flagged, "card_id").groupBy("card_country").count() query().collectAsList() // warm-up val df = query() val t0 = System.nanoTime() val (jobs, stages) = log.run { df.collectAsList() } val ms = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1e6 println() println("AQE ${if (aqe) "on" else "off"}: %d job(s), tasks per stage %s, shuffle write %,d bytes, %.0f ms" .format(jobs, stages.values.map { it.size }, log.bytesWritten(), ms)) val plan = df.queryExecution().executedPlan() if (aqe) { val text = clean(plan) val final = text.substringAfter("== Final Plan ==").substringBefore("== Initial Plan ==") val initial = text.substringAfter("== Initial Plan ==") println(" initial plan: " + planLines(initial, "Join").joinToString()) println(" final plan:") planLines(final, "Join", "QueryStage", "AQEShuffleRead", "Exchange").forEach { println(" $it") } } else { planLines(plan, "Join", "Exchange").forEach { println(" $it") } } } spark.stop() }

The estimate came from file sizes and the columns read; the filter's real result, 747 rows out of a million, was invisible to the planner. AQE off ran one job with four stages and kept the sort-merge join. AQE on ran five jobs, one per query stage: the two map sides (4 tasks each), the broadcast build (1 task), the join with the partial count (4 tasks) and the final count, merged into 1 task. Its initial plan was the same sort-merge join; its final plan has a BroadcastHashJoin fed by a BroadcastQueryStage. The shuffle write is the same 8.66 MB in both runs, because the payments' map stage had already written its files before AQE planned again. The times depend on your computer and how busy it is. On a busy laptop both runs took seconds, and the ratio is what to look at.

aside.title: Why doesn't Spark count the rows first, then plan?
aside.html: Counting means reading the data, and reading the data is most of the work the plan is meant to organise. Spark can store counts ahead of time: ANALYZE TABLE collects row counts and per-column numbers, and the cost-based optimizer in Go deeper uses them, but few teams keep them fresh. Table formats such as Iceberg (lesson 11) keep row counts for every file, which helps. AQE's measured sizes come almost free, because the map tasks had to run anyway.

sections.h: When one key is too big: skew, AQE's split and salting
sections.html:
Back to the supermarket from the opening. In the Try it, shop 7 is a marketplace, one website through which thousands of small sellers take payments, so it has 30% of a million payments. The join with the shops runs as a sort-merge join into 16 partitions. Hash partitioning, which picks a row's partition from its key, sends every row with merchant_id = 7 to the same partition, however many there are. So the median join task (the middle one, if you line them up by size) fetches 43,593 rows, and one task fetches 346,023, eight times as many. A stage ends when its slowest task ends, so 15 cores finish early and wait. That's the restaurant's trolley.

This is skew: a few keys with far more rows than the rest. The busy key is often called a hot key. The Spark UI, the web page Spark shows for a running job, gives it away: on the stage's page, the longest task runs far longer than the median.

A groupBy mostly survives skew. Each map task adds up its own rows before the shuffle (the partial sums from the last lesson). So shop 7's 300,000 payments leave the map side as four partial sums. A join has nothing to add up early: every payment row must meet its shop's row in the same task.

More partitions don't help either. Shop 7 is one key, and it lands in one partition out of 16 or out of 2,000: more tills, same trolley. Nor does speculative execution, lesson 3's backup task, where Spark starts a second copy of a slow task. The copy reads the same hot partition and is as slow. The fixes split the key itself.

The first fix is AQE's skew join. After the map stage, AQE knows every partition's size. It calls a partition skewed when it is more than 5 times the median (spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.skewedPartitionFactor) and also bigger than 256 MB (skewedPartitionThresholdInBytes). It splits that partition into pieces of about 64 MB, the advisory size, and runs each piece as its own task. Each of those tasks gets a copy of the matching partition from the other side. The plan then says SortMergeJoin(skew=true).

Three limits matter. The thresholds are sized for clusters: the demo's hot partition is a few megabytes, so with the default settings nothing happens. AQE cuts only along the edges of the blocks the map tasks wrote. Each map task wrote one block of the hot partition, and a piece is a run of whole blocks. So with 4 map tasks, the hot partition becomes at most 4 pieces. That's what the demo got with the thresholds scaled down: 16 tasks became 19, and the busiest now fetches 86,635 rows, a quarter of before. And Spark's docs describe skew handling for sort-merge joins only.

The second fix is salting: turn the hot key into several keys by hand. On the big side, add a salt, a number from 0 to N-1 worked out from the data, such as pmod(payment_id, 8) (the payment number's remainder after dividing by 8). On the small side, copy each shop row N times, once per salt. Then join on merchant_id and the salt together. Shop 7 is now 8 keys that hash to different tasks, like one trolley unpacked over 8 tills. In the demo the busiest task dropped to 125,793 rows. That isn't an eighth of 346,023, because 8 salts hashed into 16 partitions don't land on 8 different ones: a few share a partition. You pay with N copies of the small side and a few lines of code.

Salt from the data, never from a random number. When a task fails, Spark runs it again (The Spark execution model), and the new attempt must send every row where the first one did. With random salts, rows get lost or counted twice.

Before either fix, try the last lesson's. If the other side fits in a broadcast, a broadcast hash join never shuffles the big side, so no partition can be hot. Once the work is spread out, one waste is left: doing the same work twice.

try.title: Measure the hot task, then split it two ways
steps: From the labs folder, run SkewDemo. It makes a million payments where shop 7 has 30% of them, runs the join four ways and prints, for the join stage, how many shuffle rows the median task and the busiest task fetched.
Before you read: will AQE with its default settings change anything? Into how many pieces can AQE cut the hot partition, when the payments come in 4 files?
Look at the salted line. Why isn't the busiest task one eighth of 346,023?

code.title: SkewDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.batch.l08.demo import org.apache.spark.sql.Dataset import org.apache.spark.sql.Row import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.col import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.explode import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.lit import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.pmod import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.sequence import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.sum /** * A million payments, 30% of them for merchant 7, joined with 500 merchants by sort-merge join * into 16 reduce partitions. Four ways to run it, and for each one the shuffle records every join * task fetched. */ fun main() { val spark = demoSpark() spark.conf().set("spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold", "-1") // force the sort-merge join spark.conf().set("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", "16") spark.conf().set("spark.sql.adaptive.coalescePartitions.enabled", "false") // show the skew effect alone val log = TaskLog(spark) val payments = demoPayments(spark, "skewed", hotMerchant = 7) val merchants = demoMerchants(spark) fun plain(): Dataset<Row> = payments.join(merchants, "merchant_id") fun salted(buckets: Long): Dataset<Row> = payments.withColumn("salt", pmod(col("payment_id"), lit(buckets))) .join(merchants.withColumn("salt", explode(sequence(lit(0L), lit(buckets - 1)))), arrayOf("merchant_id", "salt")) .drop("salt") val cases = listOf( Triple("AQE off", mapOf("spark.sql.adaptive.enabled" to "false"), ::plain), Triple("AQE on, default thresholds", mapOf("spark.sql.adaptive.enabled" to "true"), ::plain), Triple("AQE on, thresholds scaled down", mapOf( "spark.sql.adaptive.enabled" to "true", "spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.skewedPartitionThresholdInBytes" to "1MB", "spark.sql.adaptive.advisoryPartitionSizeInBytes" to "256KB"), ::plain), Triple("salted, 8 buckets, AQE off", mapOf("spark.sql.adaptive.enabled" to "false")) { salted(8) }, ) for ((label, conf, build) in cases) { conf.forEach { (k, v) -> spark.conf().set(k, v) } val df = build().groupBy("merchant_name").agg(sum("amount_cents")) val (_, stages) = log.run { df.collectAsList() } // the join stage is the one whose tasks fetched the most shuffle records val join = stages.values.maxBy { it.sum() }.sorted() val skew = planLines(df.queryExecution().executedPlan(), "SortMergeJoin").first().substringBefore(" [").replace(Regex("""^\*\(\d+\) """), "") println("%-31s %-25s %2d join tasks, records fetched: median %,6d, max %,7d (%.1fx)" .format(label, skew, join.size, join[join.size / 2], join.last(), join.last().toDouble() / join[join.size / 2])) } spark.stop() }

try.expect:
AQE off                         SortMergeJoin             16 join tasks, records fetched: median 43,593, max 346,023 (7.9x)
AQE on, default thresholds      SortMergeJoin             16 join tasks, records fetched: median 43,593, max 346,023 (7.9x)
AQE on, thresholds scaled down  SortMergeJoin(skew=true)  19 join tasks, records fetched: median 43,619, max  86,635 (2.0x)
salted, 8 buckets, AQE off      SortMergeJoin             16 join tasks, records fetched: median 45,760, max 125,793 (2.7x)

With AQE off, the hot task fetched 7.9 times the median: shop 7's 300,000 payments plus its partition's share of the rest. AQE with its default thresholds changed nothing, because the hot partition is a few megabytes and the threshold is 256 MB. With the thresholds scaled down, the plan says SortMergeJoin(skew=true). AQE cut the hot partition into 4 pieces, one per map task (the payments are 4 files), so 16 tasks became 19, and the worst one fetched 86,635 rows. Salting needed no AQE at all and brought the worst task down to 125,793. The counts come out the same on every computer, because the demo makes the same data on every run.

sections.h: Keeping a result for a second use: cache() and its price
sections.html:
The Spark execution model ended with a cost of waiting until an action: every action runs its plan from the files again. Say the nightly job builds one result in the middle, totals per card, and runs two reports on it. That's two actions, so two scans of the files and two shuffles.

Version 1: write the middle result to Parquet files and read it back. It works, and it survives a crash, but it costs a full write plus a folder that someone must clean up.

Version 2: cache(). Calling it marks the DataFrame (Spark's table of rows) and does nothing else. The first action that computes the DataFrame also keeps each partition in the memory of the executor that computed it, as compressed batches of 10,000 rows, column by column. (An executor is the program on each worker computer that runs tasks.) From then on, Spark's cache manager looks for that plan inside every new query. A query whose plan contains it reads the stored batches instead, and the plan shows InMemoryTableScan. The match is by plan, so even a fresh spark.read() of the same files finds the cache. For a DataFrame, cache() means persist(MEMORY_AND_DISK): partitions that don't fit in memory go to the executor's local disk.

The Try it measures two shared results, each read by two reports. For totals per card, a groupBy over a million cards, the two reports took 11.0 seconds without a cache and 1.7 seconds with one. The cache saved both from repeating the scan and the shuffle. For the captured payments (those whose money has really moved), a Parquet scan with a filter, the cache barely helped. The reports took 2.7 seconds without it and 2.3 seconds with it, and filling it took 8.4 seconds, longer than both reports together. These times come from a laptop that was very busy with other work. Yours will be shorter, so compare the ratios.

So a cache has a price list:

  • The first action pays extra, to encode and store every row. Cache something that's used once and you pay for nothing.
  • A cheap source doesn't need it. Parquet with pushdown and column pruning (lesson 5) is already a fast way to read data again.
  • Cached blocks share the executor's memory with the work itself: sort buffers, lookup tables, shuffle buffers. A big cache leaves less room for the next join, which then spills to disk. When the work needs the room, Spark evicts (drops) cached blocks, and they're computed again or read back from disk.
  • The cache lives until unpersist() or until the program ends. A program that runs for weeks and caches something per request fills its executors.

Cache a result that two actions reuse, that's costly to rebuild and that fits. Then let it go. Cache it after the filter and the select, so memory holds only what the reuse needs. Call unpersist() in a finally block once the last action is done.

try.title: Cache a cheap result and an expensive one
steps: From the labs folder, run CacheDemo. For two shared results, it times two reports without a cache, the action that fills the cache, and the same two reports from the cache.
Before you read: which of the two results will gain from the cache, and which might not?
Compare the bytes in memory with the size of the Parquet files. Which is bigger, and why?

code.title: CacheDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.batch.l08.demo import org.apache.spark.sql.Dataset import org.apache.spark.sql.Row import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.col import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.count import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.sum import java.io.File /** * When cache() pays and when it doesn't. Two reports run over a shared intermediate result, with and * without a cache: first a cheap one (a filtered Parquet scan), then an expensive one (totals per * card: a shuffle of a million rows). */ fun main() { val spark = demoSpark() val path = File("build/l07/payments").absolutePath demoPayments(spark) fun ms(block: () -> Unit): Double { val t0 = System.nanoTime(); block(); return (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1e6 } fun best(block: () -> Unit) = (1..3).minOf { ms(block) } // the shared result is rebuilt by a function, so each call is a new DataFrame with the same plan fun compare(label: String, shared: () -> Dataset<Row>, reports: (Dataset<Row>) -> Unit) { reports(shared()) // warm-up val plain = best { reports(shared()) } val cached = shared().cache() val fill = ms { cached.count() } // the first action fills the cache val fromCache = best { reports(shared()) } // same plan: the cache manager swaps it in val plan = planLines(shared().groupBy().count().queryExecution().executedPlan(), "InMemoryTableScan").firstOrNull() ?: "(no cache in plan)" val info = spark.sparkContext().getRDDStorageInfo().single() println(label) println(" two reports without cache: %6.0f ms".format(plain)) println(" filling the cache: %6.0f ms (%,d bytes in memory, %d partitions)".format(fill, info.memSize(), info.numCachedPartitions())) println(" two reports from the cache:%6.0f ms plan reads: %s".format(fromCache, plan)) cached.unpersist(true) } compare("cheap: captured payments, a filtered Parquet scan (%,d bytes of files)".format( File(path).listFiles { f -> f.name.endsWith(".parquet") }!!.sumOf { it.length() }), { spark.read().parquet(path).where(col("status").equalTo("CAPTURED")) }, ) { df -> df.groupBy("merchant_id").agg(sum("amount_cents")).collectAsList() df.groupBy("card_country").count().collectAsList() } compare("expensive: totals per card, a groupBy over a million cards", { spark.read().parquet(path).groupBy("card_id").agg(sum("amount_cents").alias("total"), count("*").alias("n")) }, ) { df -> df.where(col("n").gt(2)).count() df.orderBy(col("total").desc()).limit(5).collectAsList() } spark.stop() }

cheap: captured payments, a filtered Parquet scan (14,547,753 bytes of files)
  two reports without cache:   2733 ms
  filling the cache:           8402 ms  (4,342,856 bytes in memory, 4 partitions)
  two reports from the cache:  2333 ms  plan reads: InMemoryTableScan
expensive: totals per card, a groupBy over a million cards
  two reports without cache:  10974 ms
  filling the cache:          12317 ms  (8,245,592 bytes in memory, 4 partitions)
  two reports from the cache:  1669 ms  plan reads: InMemoryTableScan

The expensive result gained more than six times on the two reports; the cheap one gained little and cost more to fill than it saved. Filling a cache is a full computation plus the work of encoding every row into column batches, so a result read only once never pays it back. The cached captured payments take 4.3 MB of memory for 250,288 rows and six columns, compressed, while the Parquet files hold all million rows in 14.5 MB: Parquet's encodings (lesson 5) are tighter than the cache's. Both plans read InMemoryTableScan once the cache is filled. Times depend heavily on your computer and on what else it's doing.

refs.title: RDD persistence and storage levels (RDD programming guide)

opening:
Picture a supermarket on a Saturday morning, with 16 tills open. Fifteen queues move quickly. At the last till, one customer is buying a restaurant's shopping for the week, and everyone behind them waits. One till got the work of eight.

Spark, the program that spreads a big job over many computers, meets this when one shop has far more payments than the rest. It sends all of a shop's payments to one task, a piece of work that runs on one processor core. It's tempting to open more tills, since that usually spreads the work. In Spark, that means more partitions (slices of the table). But the trolley still goes through one till.

In The shuffle, partitioning and joins, we saw Spark send equal keys to one task and choose a join from a guess about sizes. In this lesson, we'll watch Spark's optimizer rewrite a query and change its plan once real sizes are known. Then we'll split one busy key over many tasks, and keep a result in memory for a second use. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started at a supermarket where one restaurant's trolley held up one till while fifteen stood idle. In Spark, that's one shop's payments in one task, and more partitions don't help. AQE splits the partition once it's big enough, and salting splits the key by hand. Around that, Catalyst rewrites every query by rules, and AQE corrects its guesses at each shuffle.

Next time you run a Spark query, call explain() after the action, not before. Look for isFinalPlan=true, then for what changed from the first plan: a broadcast, a merged read, or skew=true.

Next, we'll call Spark from a program of our own, and find out what Spark 4 does with a number it can't read.

worked.title: Fix a nightly join that stalls on one task

steps.say: The nightly job joins the day's payments with a table about each shop, and it has started taking 40 minutes instead of 6. In the Spark UI, the join stage has 400 tasks: 399 finish in under 30 seconds and one runs for 35 minutes. One slow task in an otherwise fast stage is skew until proven otherwise, so find the key. (The numbers in this example are made up for teaching.)
steps.code: // 1. which keys have the most rows? (run on a sample or one day) payments.groupBy("merchant_id").count() .orderBy(col("count").desc()).show(5) // merchant_id count // 7 61,204,880 <- a marketplace: 31% of the day // 311 412,903 // 88 398,117

steps.say: First question: can the other side be broadcast? A broadcast hash join doesn't shuffle the payments, so no partition can be hot. Here it can't: the join is with a 6 GB table of risk scores per shop, far too big to copy to every executor.
steps.code: // 2. check the small side's real size before anything clever merchantRisk.count() // 92 million rows, about 6 GB: no broadcast

steps.say: Second: is AQE allowed to split the hot partition? AQE is on by default, but a partition must be over 5 times the median and over 256 MB. The hot partition is 18 GB, so it qualifies. Check the plan for the skew marker after a run. If it's there, AQE split the partition along the map tasks' blocks.

If AQE can't help (a join it doesn't handle, a skewed side with few map tasks, or a partition just under the threshold), salt the hot key by hand. Salt only shop 7, so the risk table grows by 15 rows, not 15 times.
steps.code: // 4. salt one key into 16 sub-keys val hot = col("merchant_id").equalTo(7) val p = payments.withColumn("salt", `when`(hot, pmod(col("payment_id"), lit(16L))).otherwise(lit(0L))) val r = merchantRisk.withColumn("salt", explode(`when`(hot, sequence(lit(0L), lit(15L))).otherwise(array(lit(0L))))) val joined = p.join(r, arrayOf("merchant_id", "salt")).drop("salt")

steps.say: Check with the same numbers you started from: the slowest task's rows and its time. The hot key now spreads over 16 tasks of about 3.8 million rows each.
steps.code:
// 5. check: in the stage page, max task duration should now be close to the 75th percentile
// and the join's output row count must equal the old one: salting may never add or drop a row

lab.title: Read the optimizer, split a hot key, cache on purpose
steps: Run the tests. They fail: two of the three files throw TODO, and NightlyReports runs but caches the wrong thing.

Write PlanReader.filtersBelowJoins. Walk the optimized plan's tree from the top and, once you've passed a Join, collect every Filter condition as SQL text. The test writes the filter above the join and expects your walk to find both halves of it below. Then write rulesThatFired, from the planning tracker (the record Spark keeps of which rules ran).

Write SkewedJoin.salted. The test data gives shop 7 30% of 40,000 payments, joined into 16 partitions with AQE off. The plain join's busiest task reads 13,938 rows; yours must read less than half of that and return exactly the same rows.

Write SkewedJoin.aqeSkewSettings: the settings that turn AQE on and make it treat the half-megabyte hot partition as skewed. The test runs the plain join with them and looks for SortMergeJoin(skew=true) in the final plan.
Fix NightlyReports.run. The tests check that both reports read InMemoryTableScan, that only the captured payments are cached, and that nothing is still cached after the run.
Run the tests until all eleven pass.
hints: scala.jdk.javaapi.CollectionConverters.asJava(plan.children()) gives a Java list of a step's children. Recurse with a flag that says whether a Join is above you. filter.condition().sql() gives the condition as text.

Salt from the data, not from randomness: pmod(col("payment_id"), lit(n.toLong())). On the shops side, explode(sequence(lit(0L), lit(n - 1L))) makes one row per salt. Join with arrayOf("merchant_id", "salt"), then drop("salt").

Four settings do it: spark.sql.adaptive.enabled, spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled, spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.skewedPartitionThresholdInBytes well below 500 KB (100KB works) and spark.sql.adaptive.advisoryPartitionSizeInBytes below that (64KB).
captured(payments).cache(), both reports on that, and unpersist() in a finally.
lab.done: All eleven tests in OptimizerTest, SkewTest and CacheTest pass.

drill.title: Salt a join from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write the Kotlin that joins payments with merchants on merchant_id, with every key salted into 8 keys. Then write the two lines you'd check afterwards to prove that the result didn't change.

answer.html: val n = 8L val p = payments.withColumn("salt", pmod(col("payment_id"), lit(n))) // from data: a retry gets the same salt val m = merchants.withColumn("salt", explode(sequence(lit(0L), lit(n - 1)))) // every merchant once per salt val joined = p.join(m, arrayOf("merchant_id", "salt")).drop("salt") // same rows as before, no more and no fewer check(joined.count() == payments.join(merchants, "merchant_id").count()) check(joined.columns().toSet() == payments.join(merchants, "merchant_id").columns().toSet())

recap: Catalyst holds a query as a tree and rewrites it with rules until nothing changes: filters move below joins, unused columns go, and constants are worked out once. explain("extended") shows the parsed, analyzed, optimized and physical plans.
The physical plan is chosen from size estimates, and after a filter the estimate is usually the size of the whole input.
AQE runs the plan stage by stage and plans again at each shuffle with real sizes: it merges small partitions, switches to a broadcast join and splits skewed partitions.

Skew is one key with far more rows than the rest, so one task does its work while the others wait. Broadcast if you can, let AQE split it (over 5 times the median and 256 MB), or salt the key by hand, from the data.

cache() stores a result in executor memory on its first action and puts InMemoryTableScan into later plans. It pays only when the result is reused, costly to rebuild and fits; cache after the filter and unpersist() when done.

The limit: AQE corrects only between stages, after the work is done. A broadcast it switches to has already paid for the big side's shuffle, and Catalyst still can't see inside your own functions, which the next lesson takes up.

explain.prompt: A teammate says: "AQE is on by default, so I don't need to think about joins or skew any more." Explain what AQE can and can't do, using what happens when a stage ends.
explain.answer: AQE only acts when a stage ends. Spark runs the plan one query stage at a time, and when a stage that ends in a shuffle finishes, the driver knows the real bytes in every shuffle partition. AQE then plans the rest again with those sizes. It merges tiny partitions, switches a sort-merge join to a broadcast when one side turned out small, and splits a partition that is both over 5 times the median and over 256 MB. So it fixes bad estimates, but late. A broadcast it switches to has already paid for the big side's shuffle write, because that map stage had already run; a hint that plans the broadcast up front avoids it. Its skew handling covers only sort-merge joins, only past the thresholds and only along the map tasks' blocks. So a hot key in a 40 MB partition, or one it can't split far enough, stays slow, and salting is still your tool. And it can't change anything inside a stage that's already running. AQE removes a lot of tuning, but you still read the final plan to see what it did.

deeper.html:
Catalyst's estimates can be better than file sizes. ANALYZE TABLE payments COMPUTE STATISTICS FOR COLUMNS merchant_id, amount_cents stores row counts, counts of distinct values, the smallest and largest values and counts of nulls in the catalog. With spark.sql.cbo.enabled=true, the cost-based optimizer uses them to estimate how many rows a filter keeps and to choose the order of joins (spark.sql.cbo.joinReorder.enabled). Few pipelines keep those statistics fresh, which is why AQE's measured sizes matter more in practice. Table formats help here: an Iceberg table (lesson 11) keeps row counts and each column's range of values for every file.

Two tricks at run time sit between Catalyst and AQE. Dynamic partition pruning works when a table stored in folders by a column (lesson 4) is joined with a small filtered table: Spark runs the small side first and uses its keys to skip whole folders of the big table (spark.sql.optimizer.dynamicPartitionPruning.enabled, on by default). The plan shows it as dynamicpruningexpression. Runtime filters do something similar for other columns: Spark sends a Bloom filter of the join keys to the other side's scan. A Bloom filter is a compact summary of a set that can say "definitely not in the set" for most keys that aren't.

cache() has two relatives. persist(StorageLevel) picks where blocks live: memory only, disk only, as bytes, or copied to two executors. checkpoint() writes the result to reliable storage and cuts the lineage (the recipe Spark keeps for computing it again), so a later failure never recomputes the costly part; it costs a full write, like writing Parquet yourself. And Spark 4.3 added an opt-in single-task mode for small queries (spark.sql.optimizer.singleTaskExecution.enabled), which skips shuffles entirely when the data is tiny: the optimizer deciding not to spread the work at all.
